speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved:
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Whereas the continued testing of nuclear warheads by the nuclear powers adds to the dangers of the nuclear arms race and may seriously pollute the human environment, and
Whereas the scheduled nuclear test at Amchitka is of particular concern to Canadians because of its proximity to Canada's west coast,
This Canadian House of Commons calls on all nuclear powers to cease all testing of nuclear devices, and particularly, calls on the President of the United States to cancel the test at Amchitka scheduled for this month.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am sure I speak for all members of this House and for all parties when I say how happy we are that the House has set aside time to give all hon. members an opportunity to register their support for the firm stand taken by Canada in opposition to continued nuclear weapons testing, and to the Amchitka test in particular.
The world is made apprehensive by continuing nuclear arms tests; it is becoming weary of the endless delays that are postponing a complete test ban. By this resolution, Mr. Speaker, the House of Commons, freely and truly representative of all the Canadian people, adds its voice to a universal call to the governments of the nuclear powers to have done with it.
It is a tragic comment on our world, Mr. Speaker, that even as we say this we must continue to accept the balance of nuclear deterrence as the foundation of the uneasy equilibrium that protects us all from the horror of total war. Let us hope that peace will not forever rest on such an unsure base.
This objective can be achieved slowly and with great difficulty through the continuing work of the Geneva Disarmament Committee and through imaginative initiatives such as the SALT talks, upon which so many of our hopes are centred. I doubt if it can be achieved by the detonation of more efficient bombs whether designed for offensive or defensive purposes.
In the Geneva Disarmament Committee, Canada has been working with others to find a solution to the deadlock between the United States and the Soviet Union on
the need for on-site inspections to monitor an underground test ban. Recent Canadian technical studies presented to the Geneva Committee indicate that there is excellent promise of being able to monitor, by seismologi-cal means, underground explosions other than the very smallest. Continuing research, investment in more effective monitoring facilities and improved international exchange of seismic data taken together have reduced the question of inspection to more manageable proportions.
The Canadian technical studies cannot eliminate all the uncertainties and ambiguities involved in the detection of violations and evasions of an underground test ban. The time has come, however, for the two major nuclear powers to make the effort needed to bridge the gap between them and to achieve reliable identification of those smaller seismic events that existing seismological monitoring facilities cannot classify effectively.
Unless the two major nuclear powers are willing to accept effective restraints on their arms race and on the competition in the improvement of their own nuclear weapons-as they are committed to do under Article VI of the Non-Proliferation Treaty-they cannot expect the two less highly developed nuclear powers, France and China, and the so-called "near-nuclear powers" to accept or respect the restraints of the non-proliferation agreement which the United States and the Soviet Union sponsored. That France and China should adhere to the Moscow Partial Test Ban Treaty is of the greatest importance, since it is the tests they are carrying out in the atmosphere that pose the major threat of radioactive contamination of the world environment.
The problem of verification is not yet completely solved, and the achievement of an underground test ban will take time. Until this can be achieved, both major powers should institute immediate mutual restraints to reduce the size and number of their underground tests, starting with high-yield tests like the Soviet explosion of September 27 and the proposed United States test on Amchitka Island this fall. Such measures should present no insurmountable problems of verification.
In my recent statements to the United Nations Conference on the Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy on September 6, to the Geneva Disarmament Committee on September 7, to the General Assembly of the United Nations on September 29, and in discussions with the Secretary of State of the United States and the Foreign Minister of the Soviet Union in New York on October 1 and 2, I have made Canada's position on this question abundantly clear. I have also referred specifically in the General Assembly and in my conversations with both Foreign Ministers to our specific objections to the high-yield tests, the Soviet test of September 27 and the planned United States test at Amchitka.
In the course of my meeting with Mr. Rogers, I stressed the serious concern Canadians throughout the country

October 15, 1971
Amchitka Nuclear Test
and particularly in the west feel about the Amchitka test. I dealt with the serious implications of such tests- primarily the threat posed to the world by the continuation of unrestrained testing and the consequent escalation in the nuclear arms race and the danger to the environment and ecology of the whole Pacific northwest, a danger which cannot be entirely eliminated.
These repeated, reinforced and re-emphasized representations, multilateral and bilateral alike, add force to the clear and forthright formal approach the Canadian government made to the United States government as early as last February, by way of a note that I later tabled in the House on March 29 last. I am assured by Secretary Rogers that the serious concerns of the Canadian government and people are fully appreciated by the United States administration at the highest level. The final decision on whether to proceed with the Amchitka test has not yet been taken; it is in the hands of President Nixon. There is room for hope that the United States will cancel the test, demonstrating at once their respect for the clearly expressed opinion of large sectors of its own population, millions of Canadians and men of good will in many nations, and a determination on the United States' part not to contribute to further reciprocal escalation in the nuclear arms race.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to speak on this important resolution. I begin by saying I support it strongly and predict its passage.

subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
I urge upon all hon. members that they support this declaration of opinion by this House. I am happy with the way in which this matter has been handled and am proud that my own party suggested that we devote time allotted to us in order that this important subject may be dealt with in this multipartisan way, if I may use that expression.
I must make it clear that while I favour this resolution I do not withdraw from my conviction that the Prime Minister of this country should convey directly to the President of the United States the view of Canadians on this very serious question. I regret that in the deterioration of Canada-United States relations we seem to be reduced to indirect discourse, and one wonders if the hot line has grown cold or atrophied from disuse.
While we are especially concerned about the Amchitka test which has such dangerous possibilities, we must not ignore the fact that other nations are also conducting explosions which make their grim contribution to a deterioration of some aspect of the environment. While there may be arguments about the degree of danger from fallout, there is unfortunately no doubt that the world is a little more polluted, the environment a little more poisoned, after each detonation. Thus we should call for the end of tests. As my old boss, Hon. Howard Green, used to put it at the United Nations, "We are against nuclear testing-period".

subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Because the United States is a great functional democracy and divulges to its own people and

the world its intentions and therefore allows for the buildup of public opinion, we should not appear to be concerned only with American tests and blissfully casual about the mighty explosions set off by the military machines of China, Russia and France. It is worth noting that we usually learn of the Chinese and Russian detonations when they register on the detection devices of Jodrell Bank or some other monitoring station.
Canada sometimes gets the reputation in the international community of being a "preachy" country. In this instance I like the sermon. But we must be careful that we are multidirectional in our uninvited exhortations and unsolicited precepts. For instance I could never see that British military supplies sold to South Africa were any more iniquitous than those sold by France.
Having said this, I do not hesitate in urging as strongly as I can upon the United States President the abandonment of the planned Amchitka test. The project has been given the name Cannikin and I appeal to our neighbours' leader to "can the Cannikin".
I make this appeal not because I desire that the United^ States weaken itself militarily. I cannot see how any Canadian could see any advantage for Canada in such a course. I join in this because with all its faults, all its errors and even in these strained times, I regard the United States as a great country. I would like to see it give leadership in this field as it has in so many others and make a major contribution toward the attainment of the real goal, namely, the cessation by all nations of all nuclear testing. In calling for the cancellation of this test on Amchitka Island I join not only the legislature and the people of British Columbia and other Canadians; I join a great expression of American public opinion.
Amchitka is part of Alaska, about 1,400 miles west southwest of Anchorage and therefore about the same distance from British Columbia's coast. The anxiety of the people of Alaska has been clearly expressed by the leaders of that state.
Senator Gravel said recently:
To go ahead with this test is courting a risk of magnitude we cannot determine. The risk is not worth taking. Our national security will not be imperilled if the test is cancelled.
The possibilities of serious ill effects have been outlined. Indeed, the dangers are really frightening. There is no universal law which decrees that man could not destroy himself. There is grave danger in pushing the risk too far. I would rather stop far too soon than push to the brink of an ecolocatastrophe. But apart from that we must consider the less than fatal errors we may be committing. When will we learn that we must conserve, not pillage, the heritage we have been given?
How many more species of fish must be tabbed with mercury pollution before we wake up? How much dislocation of the habitat of birdlife will we continue to tolerate? How many times must we blast and scar the earth's surface before we learn the dangers of what we are doing?
I commend those in our society who seek to awaken us to the need of giving urgent thought and urgent attention to the conservation of our environment. The voyage of the halibut boat, Greenpeace, might have been a stunt or a
October 15, 1971

gimmick. It was also a splendid and valuable dramatization of a question which after generations of environmental plundering cannot be overemphasized.
I suppose it is an oversimplification to state that a civilized people must give thought to succeeding generations. In those lands like ours which have in so many ways advanced our environmental heritage was not too well preserved by those who went before. It is our challenge to make amends. The time at our disposal is not unlimited.
With all earnestness I support the resolution moved by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). I hope we can in this special debate convey to President Nixon our genuine concern over this matter.
In this we are at one with the Congress of his own country which overwhelmingly calls for a ban on Amchit-ka. The President of the United States has many burdens, multitudinous problems, as is expected of a world leader. I fervently hope that he will enhance his stature and enlarge his influence for good by announcing that this test will not go forward-as the minister says, and he is more casual in his phraseology than I, that he will have done with it. I hope too that the other nations, not named but surely embraced in this resolution, will follow suit.

subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members know, I wrote the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) some days ago urging that such a motion be placed before the House. On behalf of my colleagues and myself I congratulate the government for having done so.
I support every word said by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). We are all very delighted that the House of Commons has been given this opportunity, I hope unanimously, to declare itself against both nuclear tests in general and the Amchitka test in particular.
I have watched the international situation, Mr. Speaker. I often think we are living in a world of insanity because of the nuclear problem. The super powers already have the capacity to destroy this earth and everything on it several times over. Yet we do not stop. We continue trying to develop bigger and stronger weapons to destroy ourselves, always with the excuse that it is being done for defensive and deterrent purposes. I deny that, Mr. Speaker.
I have a strong conviction that there are vested interests involved which are not sensitive to the needs of the world and to the dangers to peace and humanity as the result of this nuclear escalation. I think there are vested interests in the military who in peacetime cannot justify their existence unless they are constantly preparing for war which they say they hope will not happen but which at some point may happen if this kind of escalation continues. I think there are vested interests in the industrial sphere where large corporations have been tied up with the development of nuclear weapons from which they have derived great power and immense profits which they do not want to let go. I think there are vested interests in certain areas of the world which, on the Communist side, consider every western gesture as contemptible and, on the western side, consider every Soviet stance as dangerous and distrustful. There are vested interests on all sides to keep the world aflame with hate and distrust, and these are dangerous interests to our community.
Amchitka Nuclear Test
I think it is important for our civilization to say to these big nuclear powers, the Soviet Union as well as the United States and perhaps France and China, that humanity will not last if they continue with this insanity and that we as Canadian members of this Parliament plead with the nuclear powers throughout the world to finish these nuclear tests and the nuclear escalation before it gets to the point at which deterrence becomes impossible and destruction becomes inevitable.
As Canadians we are concerned particularly with the proposed test on Amchitka Island because it is close to us. I emphasize that as far as my party is concerned we are not opposed merely to the Amchitka test. That is why I was in agreement with broadening the resolution so that it would include our opposition to all nuclear testing. We are not concerned merely with Amchitka because it is close to Canada; we are concerned with the world situation.
But it is natural we should be particulary concerned and worried about the Amchitka test because the ecological and other consequences will fall immediately on our future generations. Let it be said again that we join, with all people in Canada in pleading with the President of the United States to cancel the Amchitka test. We join in this plea with those who have already spoken, with most of the people in the United States and with millions of people across the world.
I say, if I may without presumption, to President Nixon that there are moments in the life and duties of a person carrying large responsibilities when he can rise above political considerations for a moment and show leadership and imagination of a kind which will mark him in history as a great man. I say to the President of the United States that the resolution of Congress which has placed the possibility of cancelling the Amchitka test solely in his hands gives him an opportunity to show the world a mark of greatness, a mark of appreciation of the dangers of nuclear testing. I plead with him to take advantage of the opportunity for the sake of humanity and for the sake of world peace.

subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are pleased to join the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) as well as the representatives of other parties in protesting against the nuclear tests which the United States are preparing to undertake.
When danger is threatening a nation, governments forget their differences and unite with a view to objecting against the American action. Unity is still more complete as the danger is great and this is why Canada is concerned this morning. Our country is worried. We have always been, Mr. Speaker, against nuclear weapons and have always strongly objected against all nuclear tests by the so-called great powers.
Some people imagine that because the great powers are involved they can do anything, even if they endanger the existence of mankind.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we should demand of the great powers, both eastern and western, that they put an end immediately to these nuclear tests which represent a threat, as I said before, for the universe, and particularly for areas located near the testing site, such as our country.

October 15, 1971
Amchitka Nuclear Test
It is useless for me to expound lengthily on the consequences of such explosions. We have had concrete examples of radioactive fall-out. Long-term effects and radioactive fall-out are a threat not only for humans but for all forms of life.
The minister said a little while ago that the United States had not as yet arrived at a final decision. I would request the minister and the cabinet to renew, if need be, representations to the President of the United States in order that such experiences be abandoned by his country once and for all. May the United States give the example, since they can claim at this time to be the most powerful country in the world. May they put an end to those most dangerous experiences, feared by all the nations of the world.
And if the United States are experimenting improvements to the continental defence, they have no right to imperil everybody's life in anticipation of an eventual nuclear attack.
Today, in North America, a struggle must be engaged against these great powers, and it is a struggle against a form of pollution. We have already undertaken, in our areas and in our country, a fight against pollution, and today, despite all threats of air and water pollution, the greatest pollution is one to be banned forever, that is atmospheric pollution arising from nuclear blasts.
That is the first step to take, and we can then keep on working together in order to further clean the air and water of this country so that we may live here more contented and healthier.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of the Environment):
subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few brief words about the possible environmental effects of the explosion of a five megaton bomb on Amchitka this fall. These effects are likely to be pollution effects. They are likely to be ecological effects. There may not be a major earthquake resulting from this explosion or a tidal wave, but there is likely to be a pollution effect extending beyond the territorial limits of the United States.
Pollution effects have resulted from previous underground blasts. More than one in four of the underground blasts in the United States have resulted in venting-in other words, in the loss of radioactive material from below ground to the atmosphere. Statistics over the past 25 years covering some 230 underground blasts in the continental United States show that 67 have vented, some to a lesser extent, some to a greater extent. So the probability is more than one in four, if we look back on history, of a venting to the atmosphere occurring at Amchitka.
There will, of course, be contamination of ground water as well. The last underground test in the United States was carried out in Nevada approximately a year ago, on December 18, 1970. There was an accidental venting. This was not forecast. Indeed, the United States Atomic Energy Commission said that no venting could occur or would occur. In fact, venting did occur. This venting resulted in a cloud of radioactive dust which was seen locally and which moved slowly in a north and then a northeasterly direction across the United States, and

finally disappeared over Canada in the vicinity of Thunder Bay where it was knocked down by a thunder storm.
We have monitoring stations in Canada, and a few days later the radioactive level over Windsor and Toronto was found to be double the level under normal circumstances. So that the likelihood that venting will occur in the proportion of one in four is proven. The effects may be felt several thousand miles away. Certainly they are likely to be detected.
The proposed explosion of the Cannikin device at Amchitka will involve a charge 250 times as powerful as that used in the last underground test, the one in Nevada I previously described. According to the authorities I have consulted, there is no possibility that seismic waves from the explosion could do damage or even be felt in Canada, and no scientific ground exists for concern about the possibility of triggering an earthquake in western Canada. So that an earthquake is really out of the question in so far as Canadians are concerned.
These same authorities have advised me, after much consideration, that the possibility of a tsunami wave or tidal wave is relatively remote, but the element of risk to Canada cannot be quantified and complete assurance cannot be given because of the inherent uncertainties. So that while earthquake effects in Canada are unlikely, there is a remote possibility of a tidal wave.
To get to the pollution aspect, there is a one in four possibility of releases to the air. There is a certainty of contamination of ground waters in the area. Water moves through underground cracks and fissures. It is more likely to move underground in that part of the world because it is an area which is generally prone to earthquakes. It follows that ground waters which are in the immediate vicinity of the explosion on Amchitka may well seep out in time and contaminate surrounding waters. Amchitka is an island. It has a three-mile territorial limit. Underground waters eventually will percolate out from the rock under the island into the territorial waters and out into the ocean beyond the territorial limits of Alaska and therefore the United States.
In my view, this becomes a matter not only of United States concern but of international concern. It is a matter which is referred to in a general way in the Nuclear Test Ban Treaty of 1963. My reading of that treaty is that no nation can contaminate the environment beyond its own territory. This raises the question in my mind of why the United States chose to move its explosions and testing from the middle of the continental United States to a remote island, like Amchitka, surrounded by international waters.
I would again urge all members of the House of Commons to oppose this explosion, this nuclear test, not only because it is one of a possible sequence of ever larger explosions but because it could have a pollution effect and an environmental effect beyond Amchitka, that is, out into international waters as well as into the waters of the United States itself.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I wish to say I find it rather odd that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) made the speech he did in the General Assembly a short time ago and the speech in support of this motion in the House today in view of the stated declaration of policy in the government white paper on defence issued under the name of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) just a few weeks ago. I would like to say more about this if our time were not limited because there would seem to be a contradiction between the policy of one government department and another.
I wish to commend to hon. members an article which appeared in the Toronto Telegram of October 7 under the authorship of Lubor J. Zink. This article emphasizes the very point I should like to bring out, namely, that there is a contradiction of policy. Members may laugh, but let me tell the House that a few weeks ago we received the white paper issued by the Minister of National Defence which contains the following statement:
The only direct external military threat to Canada's national security today is that of a large-scale nuclear attack on North America-It is far from being the theoretically ideal means of maintaining peace, but the government, while continuing to participate in the arms control deliberations, remains convinced that there is nothing to replace it at present. Therefore. Canada must do what it can to ensure the continued effectiveness of the deterrent system-
From a potential enemy's point of view, however, North America can only logically be seen as one set of targets. Canada's centres of population and industry logically form part of the major target plan for a strategic nuclear attack on North America-
The government concluded in its defence review that co-operation with the United States in North American defence will remain essential so long as our joint security depends on stability in the strategic military balance. Canada's objective is to make, within the limits of our resources, an effective contribution to continued stability by assisting in the surveillance and warning systems and in the protection of the U S. retaliatory capability as necessary. Co-operation between Canada and the U.S. in the joint defence of North America is vital for sovereignty and security-
This over-all co-operation strengthens the U.S. retaliatory capability, and hence deterrence.
Without going further into that, I should like to say I appreciate the concern of members of the House in all parties as well as the concern of the Canadian people with regard to the Amchitka underground nuclear test. I share that concern. I believe the main reason for our concern is the potential use of nuclear power as a weapon of war.
Amchitka Nuclear Test
Let us examine the history of the atomic bomb. We know the bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki ended a war. However, the lesson which mankind apparently failed to learn from this event was that these same bombs made it abundantly clear that we must not have another war, particularly between countries that possess atomic weapons. If mankind is to survive and if the governments of the world are sincere in their search for everlasting peace, then their goal must be to abolish war, not just one weapon.
Some historians have stated that total universal disarmament and abolition of war are impossible. Nevertheless, I believe that all governments have no other choice. They must strive to seek some solution to outlaw military conflict entirely. Since 1918 I believe all reasonable people have been against war. In the years between the first and second world wars we made the mistake of believing that we could abolish military conflict by refraining from preparing for it. Unfortunately this approach, as history on many occasions has proved, was not shared by Adolph Hitler, the head of the German government of that day. These facts were revealed to all the world from the testimony of the German generals at the Nuremberg trials. It was because Britain, in particular, was so weak defensively that Hitler was prompted to start his offensive against the world. In other words, it was anticipated by Hitler that because of his modern war machinery there was no power on earth strong enough to deal with an all-out offensive by his forces. He made the assessment that no country had forces that could deter him in his goal of world domination.
I often think of the lives that could have been saved and the misery that could have been avoided if the British government had not been swayed by those who believed in unilateral disarmament regardless of the consequences. Britain at that time was considered a major world leader and as such had responsibilities, one of which was assurance to the smaller countries, particularly those in the Commonwealth group, that she was capable and prepared to protect them against aggression from a hostile force. I suggest the British government of that day either ignored that commitment of protection or at least underestimated its capabilities to produce the defence it had guaranteed.
We have been told that because of the arguments put forth by pacifist groups against rearmament and the waste of public funds on defensive measures, the British government was pressured into adopting defensive policies that were totally inadequate and to a large extent responsible for the world disaster that took place during World War II. After the events that took place during that period of our history, many governments were faced with the reality that, so long as there are hostile forces on the world scene, the only way to prevent war is to maintain equal if not superior military strength.
In the interval between the end of World War II and the present, we have not reached an acceptable solution to outlaw or prevent war. I believe the existence of a deterrent force during this period has prevented a major universal nuclear conflict. So long as one major power on the other side, be it Russia or China, has nuclear bombs and the means to deliver them, then the western nations must

October 15, 1971
Amchitka Nuclear Test
also have them, as a deterrent force. Surely the Cuban affair would confirm such a thought.
The American press informs us that the Amchitka test is important because it will be the only one made to test the Safeguard anti-ballistic missile system warhead. They also say cancellation would be read by the Soviet Union as a sign of weakness, possibly indicating that the United States is not serious about developing the anti-ballistic missile. The Soviet Union fired off a three-megaton device underground a few days ago and the U.S. test is a necessary response if the Americans are to bargain for a strong position when the strategic arms limitation talks resume at Helsinki in November.
What we in Canada must decide is, are we against just one tool of war, the nuclear weapon, or against war itself? Whichever way we decide, we must face the realities.
This House can pass all the pious resolutions or motions it wishes, and the government of Canada can make all the self-righteous protests it wants, but the fact remains that the world's dominant nations will not be listening. Under the present circumstances we are powerless to materially change the present battle for nuclear supremacy which is taking place between the world's major powers.
I believe it is about time this country stopped pussyfooting. It is about time we stood up and were counted. Either we want freedom enough to fight for it, or we do not. It is about time we made it perfectly clear we are either proCommunist or pro-democracy.
Because of the actions of this government during the past several years, no nation is sure of where we stand. There is no doubt in my mind that the United States of America is the champion of those things which we as Canadians wish to preserve: individual liberty, political freedom, the rule of law, and democratic government. Surely no Canadian can equate the United States and the Communist colossus equally in terms of Canada's interests.
There is an unpleasant mean-spirited theory current today in this country that we can have our cake and eat it too, that is, that we can enjoy all the benefits of having a guardian without doing anything to help him. Some promoters of this theory go even farther; they would even hold his arm when it is raised to ward off a blow. This criticism of the United States defence plans is part and parcel of a recent and most unsavoury national stance that Canada has adopted since 1963 when the present government came to power. Those Canadians who sincerely wish to see national freedom and individual liberty preserved have no other choice but to stand or fall with the United States. If our own history means anything to us and if we are in any way grateful for the protective umbrella under which we are now and have been living, then we should desist from destructive criticism and from the petty nagging implied in this motion put forward by the government.
It may be that there are some Canadians who look to the day of a communist triumph. This may be the reason why no official protest was forwarded by our government to other nations when it was made known that these nations were preparing nuclear tests. If those of you in

this Parliament are sincere and wish to impress the world with the sincerity of your opposition to nuclear testing, then I suggest you begin in a positive way by banning the production of all uranium within your borders. If, on the other hand, the government is using the sincerity of some hon. members on this topic for political gain or some external scheme, then it is more corrupt and dangerous than I would have believed.
Recent press reports inform us that our Secretary of State for External Affairs espoused in the General Assembly of the United Nations the cause of Communist China and complained about nuclear tests. They further stated that the Canadian minister called for an end to nuclear tests and became the first western spokesman to point the finger at the United States and the Soviet Union.
Many Canadians, as well as the people of other free countries, are wondering why he did not point the finger at other nations, such as France and Mainland China, who were known by him to have programs of a similar nature. Was he protecting Canadian uranium interests or were the countries he failed to mention preferred customers whose involvement he did not wish to disclose? We are entitled to an answer.

subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one who has been interested in the issue of nuclear tests on Amchitka for a long time, in fact as the one who first raised it in the House as early as July of 1969, naturally I am very pleased to speak today in support of the motion before us. I wish to thank and congratulate the House leaders of all parties for the successful negotiations leading to the debate today in which members have an opportunity to express their views on the lunacy of further nuclear testing by those countries described in the resolution as the nuclear powers.
I can fully appreciate the position taken by some members, particularly the hon. member who has just spoken, who sincerely feel and believe that some of us are always ready to jump on the United States for its transgressions but remain silent when some other country such as Mainland China or the U.S.S.R. indulges in similar actions.
October 15, 1971

That is one reason why I am pleased to support this all-party motion, and I hope it will pass unanimously. This motion avoids pointing a self-righteous finger at the United States alone but instead condemns further nuclear testing by any country as a threat to the human existence on this planet.
But the Amchitka blast is of urgent and pressing consideration. Understandably enough, the concern is most emphatically expressed on the west coast of both the United States and Canada, notably in British Columbia and Alaska, but I might add that Japan is a good deal closer to the test sight than is Vancouver and the Japanese are equally concerned about the test, and so are many private organizations and even American government departments.
The reasons for this opposition are, of course, fairly well known. There is the threat of earthquakes and tidal waves triggered by this five-megaton blast predicted to register at least seven points on the Richter scale, a system for measuring such explosions or earthquakes. The Atomic Energy Commission in 1969 admitted the dangers of explosions of such magnitude in a pamphlet issued in that year.
It said:
The Amchitka test area merits special attention because it is located near one of the earth's most seismically active regions. Inasmuch as earthquake mechanisms are not completely understood, no absolute statement can be made about the possibility of triggering an earthquake of large magnitude in this area.
People are also concerned about the $190 million cost of such a risky explosion to test a warhead which has already been declared by United States defence experts, or at least by some of them, as an obsolete part of the United States ABM weapon system. There is also the threat of contamination of the environment through nuclear leakage into international waters, which could poison the seabed for centuries. Finally, and most gravely, there is the contribution to the nuclear arms race that such a test will stimulate in the other nuclear countries at a time when the strategic arms limitation talks or SALT talks are progressing.
These reasons seem greatly convincing to me, and I hope they will be equally convincing to the President of the United States who is solely in charge and completely alone in deciding whether or not this horrible device is to be detonated. His is an awesome responsibility.
I have it on excellent authority that seven secret American government department reports on this topic were submitted to President Nixon of which five, including a report of the U.S. Department of the Interior, opposed the Amchitka detonation. Efforts to get copies of these reports by American elected officials such as Senator Mike Gravel of Alaska have been frustrated completely. Americans are continuing through court injuctions, appeals by elected officials and other interested people such as environmentalists and by other means to oppose the Amchitka test. I hope that this debate today will assist these Americans in persuading President Nixon to decline approval for the trigger to be pulled.
noon)
What we are discussing today is an issue so important to the future of life on this planet that our present problems
Amchitka Nuclear Test
of unemployment and other serious issues facing Canadians, as real as they are, shrink microscopically in proportion to the question of human survival that is before us. I am prepared, on the invitation of Senator Gravel, to go to Washington next Thursday with a few backbenchers from all parties-three have already agreed to accompany me- to support and assist in any way I can the American opposition to the proposed test.
I am pleased that we in this House have at least had an opportunity to discuss and debate this issue fairly fully with the co-operation of all parties. It is an issue that has grown in magnitude through the initiative of many Members of Parliament, again in all parties, and through public representations over the period of two years or more since we first raised this question until the point we have reached today.
I also hope that all appeals and especially the appeals of west coast school children will not go unheeded and that the President of the United States will listen and decide against the insanity of continued nuclear testing and, as the head of the world's major power, as the head of a state which is probably our best friend, best customer and best protector, decides that nuclear testing must be stopped and that Amchitka would be an excellent place at which to stop it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas A. Hogarth (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is extremely significant that the majority of the members who hope to be able to participate in this debate today are from the west coast. The fact that the proposed Amchitka blast is to take place on the Pacific rim is of deep concern to all west coast members, indeed to all the people living in the state of Alaska, in the territory of the Yukon and in the province of British Columbia.
I know, Sir, that the short remarks I am going to make will be made on behalf of every Member of Parliament from the province of British Columbia. We have discussed the matter sufficiently over recent weeks, regardless of our party affiliations, to be assured that each of us has done something and each of us is diametrically opposed to the proposed nuclear test at Amchitka. If other hon. members from British Columbia, on either side of the House, do not speak on this issue today it is merely because duties have taken them elsewhere and because the matter has come before the House today with some suddenness.
In the last analysis, and with the greatest respect to some of the remarks made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), I think that to a large extent the general public is becoming weary of delays in the progress with regard to the banning of nuclear testing. I think that the failure of the major governments to agree has left the peoples of the world constantly living in an atmosphere of insecurity, regardless of how remote nuclear warfare might be.
It is now 20 years since Hiroshima and Nagasaki. All of us remember the absolute terror created by the devastation of atomic bombing. The horror of the picture of what took place at that time, is still with us despite the fact it is now 20 years since that event. It is contrary to all the instincts of manking that this type of activity should ever be contemplated again, but as long as nuclear testing continues the possibility remains.

October 15, 1971
Amchitka Nuclear Test
With the greatest respect to all the diplomats in the world I think that the peoples of the world are fed up with "diplomatise", excuses, constant rationalization and constant suggestions that if they do this we might do that, and if we do that they might do this. I think this is very much brought home to us by the new generation which last week in British Columbia peacefully paraded in the streets showing their pacifism and how deeply concerned even they are about this furtherance of nuclear testing.
The news that the Amchitka blast may be set off is a drastic setback to the cause of peace. Regardless of how one looks at it, it is contrary to all common sense and it is contrary to all moral sense.
I appreciate the argument put forward by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh). It is the argument we have heard for so many years. It is the argument that leaves us still under a cloud of possible annihilation. The concept that this nation should stand and fall with the United States, is in my opinion, a concept conceived in nonsense and nurtured in possible destruction. We should always stand or fall with mankind, but regardless of what the Americans do we must do whatever we can to stop them when we think they are wrong, and the same with the Russians, the Chinese, and any other nations that pursue this course.
Apart from that concept, and apart from any environmental damage that might be caused by this blast, as set forth by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis), or the remote possibility of earthquakes or whatever may result, apart from all that I think that if President Nixon proceeds with this program it will be disastrous for the relationships between Canada and the United States. It will certainly be disastrous for those relationships on the west coast. There will set in not necessarily a hatred, not necessarily a violent anti-American reaction, but a very deep resentment, the kind that exists when your best friend has betrayed you. The good will that has been built up for almost a century with the American people will be destroyed completely.
Economic differences between Canada and the United States can be resolved. We may be resentful of what they have done but those differences can be resolved. We can survive economically. We can see their position on Viet Nam even though we do not agree with it, and it does not build resentment up among us. But for them to be indifferent to the survival of mankind because of their own nationalistic ends will leave in the people of the province of British Columbia the deepest possible resentment. It is true that the Russians are going to do testing and have done so, and also the Chinese. But we do not expect much from them. We never have. But from the United States we expect appreciation, and we expect moral evaluation, and if this test goes ahead we will not get it.
With the greatest respect, Mr. Speaker, I do not think it can be suggested that the white paper put forward by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald), in which he says we will co-operate with the United States, means co-operation to the extent of annihilation. Of course we will co-operate with the United States. Of course we realize our common interests and common destiny, but if they are going to go ahead with the destruction of the ecology and fiddle around with the whole destiny of the human race we are not going to stand idly by and co-operate.

That is the time when co-operation ceases and resistance should begin.
In that connection I am very satisfied that the people of British Columbia, certainly the people I represent who are most concerned, are properly concerned. I think they have protested in every conceivable way that could be said to be peaceful protest, and I am beginning to wonder when peaceful protest may stop with regard to actions of this kind if the United States does not react appropriately. I am quite satisfied, too, that the Members of Parliament from British Columbia in all parties have done what they can. Certainly we have all wired President Nixon, we have all spoken to Americans on the embassy staff as and when we could. The last step which the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) has suggested is a good one, but one wonders how effective it might be.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs is to be commended for the stand he has taken. The suggestion that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) should go to Washington is somewhat futile when one considers that the government, not one member of it, speaks for this nation. We should not endow the Prime Minister with some greater power than the government because he does not have it although on occasions the opposition accuses him of having it.
This debate should terminate with the unanimous adoption of this resolution representing the views of all parties, and certainly the Secretary of State for External Affairs should see to it that the United States ambassador, as a special favour to this nation, draws it to the attention of the President of the United States immediately and personally.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am going to take a little different tack as I start my remarks and I am sorry that the member for New Westminster (Mr. Hogarth) has left the chamber. I hope he really does not believe that sneering at what he called "diplomatise" is very relevant in this debate. It was George Ignatieff of Canada who at the Geneva Disarmament Conference was able to have the Soviet Union and the United States accept most features of a draft treaty presented as an alternative to a treaty that those two superpowers tried to foist upon the nations that make up that conference.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
I do not think that the cause that most of us apparently espouse, the end of nuclear testing, is helped if we allow ourselves to denigrate the real and extraordinary work done in Geneva in the last couple of years.
Ten minutes is ample time in which to express a view about the proposed underground testing of a nuclear device at Amchitka and to say that I am against all nuclear weapons testing, no matter what the excuse. As a consequence I am very pleased to support this resolution. I know that in some quarters it is considered pious for Canadian Members of Parliament to express a view on a test that should not be made unilaterally when it affects
October 15, 1971

the people of so many countries beyond the borders of the United States.
It seems to me that one of the troubles of the world today is that the meaning of words has become diminished because of the way that statesmen-to use a cliche-use them. Some years ago, with the signing of the test ban treaty, we thought the treaty meant what it said until we read the fine print and found that our bravos were really quite hollow because the fine print said that underground testing could continue.
I think the extremely clear statement made by the Minister for the Environment (Mr. Davis) on the leakage, I think the word was, from the Nevada-

subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext: Venting.

subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
I am afraid a poor lawyer has not the capacity to keep up with the language of nuclear testing but I am told the word is venting. Venting or leaking, it is an intolerable situation that any country in the world can explode a device which affects the people of other countries. It is a well known concept of common law that if I do damage to my neighbour, my neighbour has cause for action. But unfortunately there is no device by which innocent people of the world can bring an action against nations because we are still tribal people.
Surely the business of government should be that of safeguarding and fostering human life. Unfortunately the business of government has recently been preoccupied with death, with killing and being killed. Some people shrug and ask why they should bother with an issue like this when a decision has already been made. But the decision on Amchitka has not been made and I think we would abdicate our responsibilities as a concerned country if we did not make our voice heard loudly, clearly and unequivocally in Washington.
In the September 25, 1971, issue of Saturday Review that great citizen of the world, Norman Cousins, had a most interesting and helpful editorial entitled "Amchitka and Tribalism". I have not time to read it all nor would the House be interested in a long review of the editorial. However, Mr. Cousins does pose two or three interesting questions. One is, where do people turn for protection? They cannot very well complain to the United States since that government proposes to do the exploding if the decision is made. They cannot go to the International Court of Justice because unfortunately at this stage in the march toward civility that court only deals with disputes between nations. An added irony is that we are helping. One of Canada's officials is in charge of the conference to be held in Stockholm next year on the environment, but citizens of the world cannot go there to get any justice.
As the Minister of the Environment said, the pollution aspect of this test is one that concerns all of us. I should like to read to the House one paragraph of this editorial:
Here, then, is the tragic flaw in the organization of human society. The ultimate need on earth is for the protection and preservation of life. Yet no workable authority exists beyond the nation. The nation arrogates to itself the authority and the power to decide what it does not only inside but outside its borders.
This is the great dilemma which I face and the frustration I have with the United States and other countries that explode nuclear devices and do harm to innocent people because of radioactive fall-out. There is no place for the
Amchitka Nuclear Test
citizen of the world to turn as the world is now constituted. The editorial continues:
What it does inside or outside its borders may constitute, as the Amchitka test illustrates, a possible danger to other people and to the world environment as a whole. But there is no legal process by which such danger can be averted. In a larger sense, there is no legal process by which human destiny can be protected and served.
Those who know Norman Cousins know that he has tested the conscience of man during this generation. I think the challenge he has put before us is exemplified in how man is able to respond. In Geneva Mr. Ignatieff and other officials are responding in a positive way.
I share the views of those hon. members who hope that President Nixon will be apprised of this debate and will take cognizance of the views of those people in the world who would be directly affected by a decision that he alone can make.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ray Perrault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rarely in this House has there been such a degree of unanimity on an issue. Today we have heard members of all parties express their opposition and concern about the pending nuclear test at Amchitka.
What is this test at Amchitka? Canninkin is the code name for the largest underground nuclear test ever conducted by the United States. The blast would have the force of five megatons, the equivalent of 5 million tons of t.n.t. or 250 times the power of the bomb dropped at Hiroshima. It is planned, as hon. members know, for an area which is geologically unstable.
The suggestion has been made in this debate that there is a pressing American necessity for proceeding with this test. They suggest that there is virtual unanimity in the United States regarding the desirability of this test. But this view represents an utter distortion of the actual position.
There is substantial American opposition to the pending test, to the credit of many enlightened friends in the United States. The hearings which have been held in Alaska brought forth the fact that there is great opposition to the test. Indeed, only those with a special interest in defence seem to be pressing the alleged need for the test at present. Let me quote to the House the views of a spokesman for the Federation of American Scientists, the outstanding scientific group in the United States:
Jeremy J. Stone, director of the 2,000-member Federation of American Scientists, claims Cannikin was conceived by the AEC in 1966 under President Johnson to test the Spartan missile, an anti-Chinese missile defense system. However, Mr. Stone contends, the Nixon administration in early 1969 revised the ABM program to have the defense of Minuteman ICBM's against a Soviet threat as its primary purpose, with the defense of cities from a China attack as a supplemental program. "There now is ample reason to believe that a majority of the U.S. Senate will not support an anti-Chinese ABM," he says, adding that the Spartan missile isn't necessary in the ICBM defence system.
"Basically," Mr. Stone argues, "Cannikin is a bureaucratic oversight-an experiment that has been waiting to be cancelled."
The suggestion made is that the project has been tied up in military bureaucracy for a number of years and there is now no rational basis for proceeding with it.

October 15, 1971
Amchitka Nuclear Test
Other testimony developed at the Alaska hearings indicated that the defence department of the United States has announced an intention to develop an improved Spartan with a warhead of much lower yield. The improved Spartan is designed to give the Safeguard system a greater ability to intercept submarine-launched missiles as well as intercontinental missiles. Many defence planners believe, according to testimony given, that in essence there is nothing important which the basic Spartan can do that the improved Spartan cannot do better.
It is really difficult to come to any conclusion except that certain military planners in the United States want to proceed with the test merely for the sake of going ahead with it. The events which may have provided justification for the test at one time have now passed. We are particularly concerned in the Canadian northwest with this United States proposal for testing at Amchitka. Our view in no way should be construed as one that would tolerate, on the other hand, nuclear testing by other nations. All testing poses a danger to man, and it is fallacy to suggest that any part of the world can remain immune from the effects of testing, be that testing atmospheric or underground.
In 1969, when I was with the Canadian delegation at the United Nations, I had an opportunity to serve on a committee which reviewed the report of the United Nations Scientific Committee set up to determine the effects of nuclear radiation. The UNSCEAR Committee was formed in 1955. It is made up of scientists of many nations. Canada, the U.S.S.R. and the United States have representatives on the committee. Despite major differences in the ideologies of the countries represented on the committee these scientists agreed, on the basis of scientific evidence which they had collected, that even underground testing poses the risk of environmental pollution. These scientists from all over the world expressed concern about the possibility of brain damage to unborn children resulting from radiation.
They warned that severe damage to the nervous system can be caused by radiation, whatever the source of that radiation may be. They pointed at the real danger of severe mental retardation in these unborn children. Exposure to radiation may result in an increase in the number of chromosomal aberrations, they say. These aberrations, we are told, are clearly of genetic importance and may in fact comprise the major component of the genetic damage resulting from radiation exposure. World scientists are engaged now in the process of checking the findings gathered thus far, findings which indicate that the very chromosomes which decide the future genetics of mankind and the ability of man to survive are affected by nuclear radiation.
According to a report recently issued by Professor Ernest Sternglass, professor of radiation physics at Pittsburgh University school of medicine, the deaths of 400,000 children in the United States and 100,000 children in Britain had resulted from nuclear tests in the mid-1960's in the United States and Britain. He estimated that 10,000 die with each megaton detonated in atmospheric testing.
In the face of this kind of counsel by world scientists, what has been the Canadian government's actions? I would remind those who are critical of the Canadian government's position that no nation has spoken out more (Mr. Perrault.]
vigorously against all nuclear testing than this nation and no government has spoken out more vigorously than the Canadian government. On many occasions the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) has made representations at the Geneva Disarmament Conference, at the United Nations and at the intergovernmental level. He has expressed the continuing Canadian concern and opposition to nuclear testing on the part of any nation in the world. This opposition has not been restricted to testing by the United States; it has been extended to and includes other nations.
Some critics suggest that the Prime Minister of this country has remained silent and has been unwilling to make any representations in this field.

subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext: Who has suggested that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
They either do not know or neglect to observe that on October 17, 1970 the Prime Minister said:
-the whole problem of nuclear testing is being discussed and Canadians aie saying things and the government and its representative in Geneva are talking very much about this. We have advanced certain means-if we can agree to the prohibition, for instance, of underground testing. We have advanced certain Canadian devices which will permit to police this prohibition. Therefore we are very much concerned with it-
Then he commented about the Amchitka Aleutian test and said that we object, using these words:
-some people rightly or wrongly think that there would be a direct menace to the lives on the west coast.
The Prime Minister then went on to say:
We have taken the position that we want a moratorium on testing; we want the countries of the world to stop their testing. We have added support to the strategic arms limitation talks. We have encouraged both the U.S.S.R. and the U.S.A. to get on with them. We have participated actively in all the discussions on nuclear bans in Geneva. We are a member of the 18-nation disarmament conference. We are as active as we can be in them, but we cannot yet dictate policy to the countries which are proceeding with these tests. But we are a signatory, as you know, to the non-proliferation treaty and we are trying to get other countries to sign it-
That shows just some of the efforts made by the Canadian government in recent months and years. Clearly, this government is opposed to testing in any form on the part of any nation in the world. We have provided this kind of leadership because we are convinced that the future of mankind is threatened not only by underground tests at Amchitka but by tests conducted by other nations including the Soviet Union, the People's Republic of China as well as by the atmospheric testing carried out by France.
We are all concerned about the possible effects of nuclear radiation. No one can feel complacent about nuclear testing, and it does not matter who does the testing and what form the testing takes. The pending Amchitka test is just as deplorable as the Soviet tests which were undertaken a few days ago. The sooner the people of the world make known their absolute opposition to testing by any country, the better will be the chance that battered mankind will be able to survive. It is gratifying to see the unanimity in the House at this time on this question.

subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two particular reasons why I wish to add a few words to the discussion today on the resolution before us calling for the halting of nuclear tests in general and the
October 15, 1971____________________COMMONS DEBATES_______________________________________8745
cancellation of the Amchitka underground nuclear test in particular. My first reason stems from the fact that I have recently returned, along with other hon. members of the House, from Washington. We went to one of the national parks of the United States and spent a whole week in an intensive appraisal of the operation of the United States national parks system. During the course of that week we had the opportunity to participate in discussions with the top people in their national parks service. These people are dedicated to the preservation in perpetuity of natural beauty in an unpolluted state in some of the choicest areas that lie within the boundaries of our neighbouring country. We also had an opportunity of meeting with members of the National Advisory Council on Parks, a very interesting and important body of citizens in the United States. We had discussions with the heads of all the great voluntary national conservation organizations in the United States, organizations comprised of thousands of citizens.
As a result of that experience I am much more aware than I might otherwise have been of the fact that literally millions of President Nixon's fellow citizens are today hoping and praying that he will see fit to cancel the Amchitka test. They will be encouraged and happy because of the fact that a motion in the terms now before us is being discussed in the Canadian House of Commons. This is one reason why it is most fortunate and opportune that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) has today brought forward this motion for discussion and, hopefully, unanimous endorsation, by the Canadian House of Commons.
I am not going to attempt to cover the ground that some of the previous speakers have covered with regard to the broad issues involved in nuclear testing, underground or otherwise. In speaking as they have in this chamber today they have spoken not only on behalf of all Canadians, not only on behalf of citizens in other places throughout the world, but have also voiced the sentiments that I know are held by many millions of citizens in the country to the south, our closest neighbour, upon whose executive head has been placed the responsibility of deciding whether this test will be carried out.
My second reason for wanting to say a few words is that, if there are immediate disastrous results from this test should it take place, it is my constituents who will be in the first line of fire. I have a very vivid recollection of the events on a certain Easter weekend not many years ago. As a result of a natural earthquake in Alaska and the tidal wave resulting therefrom, many citizens and many communities in Comox-Alberni suffered disastrous effects. The present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing), who visited the area shortly afterwards as a member of the Canadian government, can confirm what I am saying. The memory of that situation is still very fresh in the minds of the residents of Comox-Alberni who suffered from the effects of that tidal wave.
Many reputable scientists have said there is a possibility that the effect of this underground nuclear explosion in the proportions which are contemplated could directly or indirectly trigger another earthquake or tidal wave. When the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) spoke earlier he suggested that the possibility of direct earthquake
Amchitka Nuclear Test
effects is remote. The advice he has received may very well indicate that this is the case. I certainly hope this is so. He did indicate there is a possibility that there might be a resulting tidal wave. This is one of the reasons why my constituents in particular are gravely concerned about the possible results that may flow from this underground nuclear explosion if President Nixon does not cancel it. My constituents in particular are hoping and praying that they will not be subjected to an avoidable tidal wave. We recognize the fact that we live in one of the more unstable geological regions of the world and that there is always the possibility of a major earthquake and tidal wave which may affect us. However, we feel it is complete insanity for man to accelerate or increase the possibility of that kind of event taking place.
We also recognize that the other pollutant effects to which the Minister of the Environment referred briefly, if they affect Canadians, will affect us as quickly and probably with more impact than any other part of the country. This is further reason for our opposition to this event taking place. It is further reason why the residents of Comox-Alberni, almost to the last individual, are completely in support of the resolution introduced today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
We all recognize the fact that the decision is not ours. We realize that this motion is only an expression of opinion. However, I hope the remarks that have been made by the members who preceded me and who have gone into various aspects of the matter will be an indication that we have seriously assessed this question from many sides. I hope that through the appropriate channels the discussion we are having today in the Canadian House of Commons will be brought to the attention of the President of the United States and that he will give it proper weight in his consideration leading to the decision which he has been asked to make by the Congress of the United States.
I hope this resolution will be passed unanimously and that shortly there will be an announcement which will enable us all to breathe a little more freely.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul St. Pierre (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF OPPOSITION OF HOUSE OF COMMONS TO AMCHITKA AND OTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether we have not seen today how much virtue there can be in short speeches. We are nearing the end of two hours of debate but even so we have heard almost every aspect of this question canvassed and canvassed very thoroughly. Ten minute speeches have been the rule and I believe that as a result those who have taken part have concentrated their thoughts more closely than usual and have, frankly, made better speeches than they would have made had they used 20 or 30 minutes. I intend to attempt to use less than ten minutes, possibly only five.
It is not my purpose to attempt to cover ground which has been so ably covered by speakers on both sides of the House. I wish to deal only with one small aspect of this matter which I have not yet heard raised during the debate. I believe it strengthens the decision which this chamber is, hopefully, about to take unanimously. I should like to raise the question whether the proposed blast at Amchitka would not constitute a violation by the United States of the nuclear test ban treaty. I want to read

October 15, 1971
Amchitka Nuclear Test
a section of this treaty, paragraph (b) of article I. For the sake of clarity I will have to read paragraph (a) first. It states:
1. Each of the Parties to this Treaty undertakes to prohibit, to prevent and not to carry out any nuclear weapon test explosion, at any place under its jurisdiction or control.
(a) in the atmosphere; beyond its limits, including outer space; or underwater, including territorial waters or high seas; or-
This is the significant section for my purposes:
-(b) in any other environment if such explosion causes radioactive debris to be present outside the territorial limits of the State under whose jurisdiction or control such explosion is conducted.
The section continues, but the foregoing is the significant point, Mr. Speaker.
The blast at Amchitka will in all probability cause pollution of ground water at the very least and it is almost inconceivable that this contaminated water will not extend beyond the three-mile territorial limit of United States waters. It is inconceivable upon the evidence-and I refer now to the figures given earlier by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis)-if there is leakage into the atmosphere as occurred in 67 out of 230 tests in Nevada, one out of every four, that this contamination would not be carried in the atmosphere into Canada.
The United States is not, of course, the country most grievously at fault in this matter. The Chinese and the French have been detonating in the atmosphere itself and we know from our pollution readings that when they do radioactivity increases in the Canadian skies. But those countries are not signatories to the test ban treaty. The United States is. I suggest there is a serious question to be raised as to whether the United States, if it proceeds with the Amchitka test, would not be in violation of the treaty it has signed.
There are others, Mr. Speaker, who wish to be heard in this debate. I shall take my seat in a moment. I hope Parliament will express itself unanimously in favour of this resolution. Perhaps parliamentarians of other nations will also speak up as this Parliament is doing and speak for the people of the world. I trust that our voices will be heard and heeded. I thank hon. members for their attention.

time could be so spent. If I may say so without partisanship, that is something of a sacrifice when one considers there are so many opportunities of usefully spending opposition days.

Mr. Speaker, before discussing this amendment I have what is probably a question of privilege in connection with the obligations of the government to file the annual financial statements of Northern Canada Power Commission. The financial statements of the commission are prepared to the end of March each year, and by the laws of the country the government is required to table these financial statements each year. This year, the current financial statement of the commission was tabled on October 8.
In addition to the tabling requirement there is a requirement that the report receive certification by the Auditor General. Quick reference to the document tabled in this House on October 8 will reveal that because of the highly unsatisfactory state of the commission, the Auditor General withheld his approval of the financial statement.
The financial report that should have been filed normally consists of a breakdown, by plant, of the operating expenses of the plant and of the income received as a result of its operation. In the document that was filed on October 8 that statement is missing. During the last three years I have had to write to and call officials in the department and in the commission. I wanted them to produce that independent station-by-station breakdown which they are required to keep under the provisions of the Northern Canada Power Commission Act. I submit that the station-by-station, or plant-by-plant breakdown is part and parcel of the financial statement of the commission. Since it was not available, the Auditor General withheld certification of the document that was tabled on October 8. That was one of his reasons.
My question of privilege resolves itself to this: the commission, or the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) through whom the commission reports to Parliament, has not complied with the law as set out in the Northern Canada Power Commission Act and has not tabled the financial statement that the law requires to be tabled.
We cannot debate intelligently requirements under the Northern Canada Power Commission Act, the legislation which the government is trying to amend, unless the existing law is complied with. One provision of the act, as I have said, requires each plant in the system to be self-sus-

taining. We have no way of knowing whether plants within the system are self-sustaining unless an individual, plant-by-plant breakdown is tabled as part and parcel of the accounts of the commission.
Information required by law to be tabled in Parliament has been withheld from Parliament. That omission, in my submission, ought to be rectified immediately before we continue this debate. The withholding from the House of information which is required by law to be tabled by the minister, any government official or government agency, constitutes a breach of the privileges of this House. That information has not been made available.

I do not think that this question of privilege is in order. [English]

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERS FUNDS FOR INVESTIGATION OF PROJECTS, ADVANCES FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
I have listened to the hon. member's presentation, and although he may have a grievance I do not think the matter can be brought under the umbrella of breach of parliamentary privilege. The hon. member submits that the minister or someone on behalf of the government is in breach of the law in that there has been a failure to file a document.
Although I appreciate that any such omission may complicate the consideration of a piece of legislation before the House, I do not think it can be considered to be a breach of parliamentary privilege which can give rise to a motion and the referral of the matter to a committee. Even if that were the case, I suggest to the hon. member that the matter which is before the House would still be before us and we would have to consider the amendment standing in the name of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). I do not think I can be of much assistance to the hon. member with regard to his suggestion that the matter be considered by way of breach of parliamentary privilege.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERS FUNDS FOR INVESTIGATION OF PROJECTS, ADVANCES FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
With great respect, perhaps Your Honour's lack of knowledge of the Northern Canada Power Commission Act, the government's amendments now before us and my amendment has prevented the Chair from appreciating the full import and seriousness of the omission in this case. Each year so far the provisions of the Northern Canada Power Commission Act have been complied with. A full and complete financial disclosure has been made and the commission's financial statement has been tabled. This is the first year in which the commission and the government have departed from that course.
There is no way for us to debate this bill intelligently, in light of amendments before the House, unless we are given the type of information that I hold in my hand. This
October 15, 1971

information was tabled last year; it is part of the financial statement. It is entitled "Northern Canada Power Commission statement of income and expenses for the year ended March 31, 1970". This is a three-sheet breakdown of income and expenses, by plant. We cannot intelligently consider the amendments before the House unless the current information is placed before us and the minister is prepared to table it immediately. Only if that is done can I and others wishing to participate in this debate compare the information on an annual basis. If the information is not made available immediately, I am prepared to move the adjournment of the House until such time as the minister brings it foward, as he is required to do by law.
